answer: Here's the rest of the story. New cells made at the tips of shoots and roots (the apical meristems) make the plant longer. This is called primary growth. Woody plants also have side meristems, the vascular and cork cambium, that make stems and roots thicker. That thickening is called secondary growth, and it's what produces wood [2]. Most of the actual increase in size comes from cells getting bigger, not just from more cells. The hormone auxin makes cell walls loosen by pumping acid into them, water flows in, and each cell stretches like a balloon [1][3]. As these cells grow, they turn into specialized tissues. Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots, and phloem carries sugars from the leaves [1][2]. Auxin also drives the plant's responses to its surroundings. Stems bend toward light because cells on the shaded side grow longer, and roots grow downward in response to gravity [1].

sources.title: The Acid Growth Theory of auxin-induced cell elongation is alive and well
